planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into moist, calcareous soil along a streambank, gravel bar, or wet meadow in full sun to very light shade; shining ladies' tresses is the earliest-blooming Spiranthes across most of its eastern North American range and needs the same wild mycorrhizal fungi present in its native sites, so wild collection is never appropriate.

directions: Shining ladies' tresses grows naturally along calcareous streambanks, lakeshores, and wet meadow seeps from the Maritimes and Great Lakes south into the Appalachians, favoring consistently moist, mineral-rich soil in full sun. It flowers earlier than most other Spiranthes in its range, from late spring into midsummer, producing a short, dense, single spiral of small white flowers whose lip is marked with a distinctive bright yellow-orange center, giving the spike a glossy, luminous look. Once established in a bog garden or constantly damp rock garden pocket, clumps slowly increase but resent root disturbance, so leave plantings undivided for several years. Keep soil wet to consistently moist through the growing season and avoid fertilizer or heavy organic mulch, which disrupts the fungal partnerships the plant depends on.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; lace-lip ladies' tresses is a tall coastal-plain wetland species found in wet pine savannas, bogs, and roadside ditches from the Gulf Coast up the Atlantic seaboard and needs consistently saturated soil year-round.

directions: Lace-lip ladies' tresses is a tall, slender native orchid of wet pine savannas, bogs, and seasonally flooded ditches across the southeastern coastal plain from Texas to the Carolinas. It blooms in late summer, producing a loose, somewhat lax spiral of white flowers whose lip is finely fringed along the margin, the feature that gives the species its common name. It needs permanently wet, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun and does poorly in any planting that dries out even briefly, making a constructed bog bed or pond margin a better fit than an ordinary perennial border. Leave established colonies undisturbed, since like other Spiranthes it depends on specific soil fungi that are easily damaged by transplanting.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; Case's ladies' tresses is a small boreal species of open sandy clearings, lakeshores, and roadsides across the northeastern US and eastern Canada and does not tolerate rich, wet garden soil the way bog-dwelling Spiranthes do.

directions: Case's ladies' tresses is a diminutive native orchid of open, sandy or gravelly ground in the northeastern United States and eastern Canada, found on lakeshores, barrens, and disturbed roadside soil rather than wet bogs. Unlike most Spiranthes, it prefers lean, well-drained, acidic soil that is only lightly moist, and it flowers in late summer with a short, tight spiral of small white flowers. It suits a sunny, sandy native plant bed or rock garden setting rather than a constructed bog, and established plants should be left undisturbed since the roots depend on a specific soil fungus. Avoid fertile garden soil or heavy mulch, both of which favor competing vegetation over this small, slow-growing species.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in spring into permanently moist, calcareous soil in full sun to part shade; marsh helleborine spreads by creeping rhizomes in fens and wet meadows across Europe and temperate Asia and is one of the more garden-amenable hardy terrestrial orchids offered by specialist hardy-orchid nurseries.

directions: Marsh helleborine is a creeping, colony-forming hardy orchid native to calcareous fens, dune slacks, and wet meadows across Europe and temperate Asia, where it spreads steadily by rhizomes to form sizeable patches over time. In early to midsummer it bears loose spikes of nodding flowers with brownish-purple sepals and a crimped white lip veined in pink, giving the spike a frilled, delicate look unlike the more somber flowers of its woodland relative E. helleborine. It needs permanently wet, mineral-rich soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the fen and marsh conditions where it grows wild, and resents drying out even briefly. Because it spreads vegetatively, a single nursery-propagated division can be used to start a colony in a constructed bog bed or pond margin over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into moist, calcareous, humus-rich soil in part shade; this naturally occurring hybrid between C. parviflorum and C. candidum arises where the two parent species overlap in calcareous fens and prairie remnants of the upper Midwest and is intermediate between them in size and color.

directions: Cypripedium ×andrewsii is a naturally occurring hybrid between yellow lady's slipper (C. parviflorum) and small white lady's slipper (C. candidum), first described from the calcareous fens and prairie remnants of the upper Midwest where the two parent species grow together. It is intermediate between its parents, typically producing a pale yellow to greenish-yellow pouch smaller than typical C. parviflorum but larger than C. candidum, on plants of moderate height. Like both parents, it requires calcareous, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist without becoming waterlogged, in dappled or part shade, and depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi present at the planting site. Only use nursery-propagated divisions, never wild-collected plants, and avoid disturbing an established clump once it is settled.
sources: Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)
